title: Two final attributes of the best learning-focused leaders and managers we have seen across the world.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This post completes a three-part list of seven attributes shared by the learning-focused school leaders and managers Skelton and colleagues have observed internationally. The sixth attribute is embracing simplicity: in busy schools, leaders keep everyone focused on a few things that matter and resist the fearful busyness that avoids saying no. The seventh is modelling what matters, because repeated experiences create symbolic reputations, and leaders who talk a good game but do not walk the talk damage trust in their schools. Skelton draws on Jim Collins' Hedgehog Concept and on his own experience of spending time in classrooms with his deputies as a visible signal of priorities. He admits the seven attributes are not exhaustive, and closes with a reflective checklist covering classroom time, coaching, simplicity and modelling.
points: Simplicity is presented as harder than busyness, since busyness lets leaders avoid saying no and avoid accountability.
Busyness is reframed as a mark of fear rather than virtue, and cognitive overload follows when messages multiply.
Leaders are judged symbolically as well as technically, and consistent behaviour builds a reputation that is hard to shift either way.
Walking the talk means being seen in classrooms and engaging in conversations about learning, which both gathers evidence and signals priorities.
The closing checklist gives leaders concrete self-audit questions, such as how many classrooms they have spent thirty minutes in over five weeks.
quotes: Simplicity matters. It enables focus and clarity, reduces cognitive overload and increases the chances of building coherence and consistency, consent and consensus in any organisation, including, and perhaps especially, schools.

Schools are very busy, active places. There is always something going on. The movement of students, the constant beginning and endings of lessons, the hourly changes of teachers, classes and subjects, the different parental, student and community stakeholders; all these and more add together to create places where the opportunity to lose focus presents itself every hour of every day.

Paradoxically, creating the rigour that underpins simplicity is harder than allowing busyness and its impending chaos to run rife. Busyness and a lack of focus help us not to have to say ‘No’ to anything; help people not to be held to account; help to fudge the focus on clear outcomes; help to, in the short term, stop people being annoyed and disappointed. Busyness can look like a characteristic of the virtuous when it is actually a characteristic of the fearful.
Talking a good game’ is not a complimentary phrase; it almost always means not delivering on what you say you believe in.
When repeated consistently, talking a good game becomes something negatively symbolic about an organisation. When a symbol has become established, it acts as a short-cut to our feelings.
What this means is that rather than talk a good game, these leaders and managers walk the talk. They embody through their actions not only technical proficiency but symbolic power, too.

That’s the reason why, if we claim that our school is passionate about learning, leaders and managers have to walk the land, often. Which student or parent or teacher is going to believe in a passion for learning if they barely see a leader or a manager who looks even vaguely interested in classroom learning or doesn’t engage in conversations about learning when they have been in classrooms?
